title: A fence around the Torah
hook: rabbis add protective rules around Torah laws

segments.voice: Yesterday, minhag, and your line: custom is law too. Did you follow someone else's custom in their space? Today, rules built on purpose, not by habit: fences. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

At the top of a cliff there's a beautiful view, and a sheer drop. Nobody puts the warning sign at the edge itself. By the time you're reading a sign at the very edge, one bad step is all it takes. So the railing goes in a few feet back. You can still see everything. You just can't stumble over. And the railing changes how people walk: they lean, they look, they relax. It isn't the cliff. It's what keeps you from the cliff. The opening teaching of Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, asks the sages to build one of these. Today's word is that railing.
screen: `A VIEW, AND A DROP.` → `THE RAILING GOES IN FEET BACK.` → `NOT THE CLIFF, THE RAILING.`

segments.voice: Seyag. It's the Hebrew word for a fence, and in Jewish law it names a protective rule the sages add around a Torah law to keep people from breaking it. Start with the source. The first mishnah of Avot tells the sages to be careful in judgment, to raise up many students, and to make a fence around the Torah. Second, what one looks like. On the Sabbath, as the sages read the Torah, a person may not carry things out from a house into the street. The Mishnah in tractate Shabbat adds a rule for Friday: a tailor shouldn't go out with his needle close to dark, in case he forgets it's there and carries it once the Sabbath begins. Going out with a needle on a weekday afternoon isn't the problem. The fence sits a little way back from the edge. Third, fences can go too far, and the tradition says so itself. In the garden, God told Adam not to eat from the tree. But when Eve repeats the command, she adds something: "neither shall ye touch it." A teaching in Avot de-Rabbi Natan imagines Adam built that fence, and the serpent used it. It pushed her against the tree: you touched it and nothing happened, so eating won't hurt either. The lesson the sages draw is plain: don't make the fence more important than what it guards, or when the fence falls, the garden goes with it. Fourth, fences aren't only legal. Rabbi Akiva, also in Avot, names others: tradition is a fence for the Torah, and silence is a fence for wisdom. A fence is a kindness to your future self. A fence around the law.
screen: `MAKE A FENCE AROUND THE TORAH.` · `THE TAILOR'S NEEDLE BEFORE DARK.` · `NEITHER SHALL YE TOUCH IT.` · `SILENCE, A FENCE FOR WISDOM.` · then, large: `A FENCE AROUND THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is building one fence around a good habit. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you want to protect: sleep, a morning walk, kind words, an hour without a screen. Now find the cliff edge, the moment it usually slips away. Then move a few steps back from it. What small rule, set earlier, would keep you from the edge? Phone out of the bedroom. Shoes by the door. Make it small and clear. And remind yourself which is the fence and which is the garden. The bell holds the time.
Seyag. A fence: a protective rule the sages set around a Torah law, so people stay far from breaking it. Today's word.
Your line: a fence around the law. Today, put up the small fence you chose, and once, check that you still know what it's guarding. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Rabbinic rules often work as fences: for example, the sages added Sabbath rules that keep people well back from the work the Torah forbids, and Jews who keep them treat the fences as part of the law.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rabbis just made the rules stricter.
what it means: a fence: a protective rule set back from a Torah law, so people don't stumble into breaking it.
what a scholar hears: Avot 1:1, Shabbat 1:3's tailor and his needle, and Avot de-Rabbi Natan's warning that Adam's fence, 'neither shall ye touch it', let the serpent in.

notes: Please confirm JPS 1917 Genesis 3:3 reads 'neither shall ye touch it'.
Avot 1:1 paraphrased (be deliberate in judgment, raise up many disciples, make a fence for the Torah).

Berakhot 1:1 paraphrased: the sages' limit 'until midnight' 'to distance a person from transgression'; Rabban Gamliel's view (until dawn) not mentioned. The phrase 'the Torah's evening Shema may be said all night, by the sages' reading' summarizes the mishnah's end; please confirm.
Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 1 (version A) paraphrased: Adam's fence ('do not touch'), the serpent pushing Eve against the tree. Please confirm the version and that the lesson drawn is fair.
Avot 3:13 (numbering varies; 3:17 in some editions): Rabbi Akiva on fences (tradition for Torah, tithes for wealth, vows for abstinence, silence for wisdom). Only two are named.
The voice says 'the first mishnah of Avot'; this is the cited text's own position, not a ranking.
